metadata.title: Recommendations to Reduce the Risk of Transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) by Human Cells, Tissues, and Cellular and Tissue-Based Products (HCT/Ps): Draft Guidance for Industry
metadata.topic: Draft guideline · FDA human drugs and biologics

candidates.statement: We, FDA, are issuing this guidance to assist you, establishments making donor eligibility 18 (DE) determinations, 1 in understanding the requirements in 21 CFR part 1271, subpart C (21 19 CFR part 1271, subpart C). The regulations under 21 CFR part 1271, subpart C, set out 20 requirements for determining donor eligibility, including donor screening and testing, for 21 donors of human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products (HCT/Ps). 2 This 22 guidance provides recommendations for screening donors for evidence of, and risk factors 23 for, infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the organism that causes tuberculosis. 24 The guidance also recommends additional steps that HCT/P establishments should take to 25 reduce risk of transmission of Mtb until such time as appropriate FDA-licensed, approved, or 26 cleared donor screening tests are available for use to test donors for Mtb infection. 27
candidates.context: FDA identified a safety concern when investigating reports of Mtb infections in recipients of 30 allograft bone products. 3 These multi-state outbreaks indicated that there is a risk of 31 transmission of Mtb infection by HCT/Ps. This guidance, when finalized, will identify Mtb 32 as a relevant communicable disease agent or disease (RCDAD) as defined in 21 CFR 33 1271.3(r)(2) and will supplement the recommendations contained in other DE guidance 34 documents for donors of HCT/Ps. 4

candidates.statement: There are FDA-approved diagnostic products that can detect an immune response to 222 TB antigens; examples include FDA-approved purified protein derivative (PPD) of 223 tuberculin antigens injected intradermally for the tuberculin skin test (TST), and 224 interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) blood tests (e.g., T-SPOT.TB test and 225 Quantiferon-TB Gold Plus test). Both types of tests measure immune sensitization to 226 mycobacterial protein antigens that occurs following exposure to mycobacteria, and 227 these tests should be used in conjunction with clinical risk assessment, radiography, 228 and other medical and diagnostic evaluations to aid in the diagnosis of Mtb infection. 229 These additional medical and diagnostic evaluations are essential to diagnosing TB 230 disease and LTBI. When using the TST and IGRA tests, the person tested must have 231 viable intact immune cells to produce an accurate result, which makes them 232 impractical for evaluating TB risk for a cadaveric (non-heart beating) donor. A variety 233 of factors can affect TST and/or IGRA test performance, including recent infection 234 (i.e., testing before a cell-mediated immune response has developed), age, receipt of 235 Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccine (can affect TST but does not affect IGRA), 236 and impaired immunity, specifically, T-lymphocyte mediated cellular immunity (Refs. 237 130-136). Negative tests results do not exclude LTBI or TB disease. 238
candidates.context: There are currently no FDA-licensed, cleared, or approved donor screening tests for 217 use in testing HCT/P donors for evidence of Mtb infection. However, a donor’s 218 medical record or medical history may include results of other tests for detection of 219 immune response to or presence of Mtb, which are discussed below. 220 FDA-cleared diagnostic tests, such as nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT), 240 including PCR tests, for the detection of Mtb in respiratory specimens (e.g., sputum) 241 are also available. The results of such tests are not intended to be used in isolation and 242 are to be used as an adjunct to other laboratory tests and clinical findings. 8 A negative 243 result does not exclude TB disease (Refs. 17, 31, 127-130). We note that PCR testing 244 of a bone product from an infected donor has not consistently provided the level of 245 sensitivity necessary to identify presence of Mtb (Refs. 31, 85), and FDA has not 246 authorized a PCR test for the detection of Mtb using a bone specimen. 247 7 In 2007, FDA identified sepsis as a RCDAD, requiring screening of HCT/P donors for risk associated with sepsis).
